items.context: The research item description says 'Output: domain model doc for greenfield rewrite' and explicitly excludes technical choices (n8n, Postgres/Redis, providers). But it does not specify whether the conclusion should also include skeleton proto schemas (since the initiative has already decided proto lives at packages/proto/schemas/notification-hub/v1/) or just a prose domain model. This affects how much depth round 2+ needs and whether a separate execute item is needed for the proto contract.

options.label: Domain model doc only — prose + tables + state diagrams; proto authoring is downstream work folded into execute/notification-hub-greenfield-core
options.rationale: Keeps the research output focused on the 'what concepts to preserve' question; defers schema syntax bikeshedding to execution; simpler to converge

options.label: Domain model doc + skeleton proto files (notification.proto, profile.proto, device.proto, subscription.proto) with messages and enums but no service definitions
options.rationale: Forces concrete decisions on enum values and field names while domain context is fresh; produces a more directly actionable handoff but expands research scope

options.label: Domain model doc + new backlog item execute/notification-hub-proto-contract scoped specifically to authoring the v1 proto
options.rationale: Separates concerns cleanly — research stays prose, proto authoring becomes its own first-class item with its own acceptance criteria

items.topic: Fate of the legacy NotificationCategory enum (17 values)
items.context: The legacy notify code defined a closed enum of 17 product-shaped categories (AccountCreditsOrApi, Award, IssueStatus, Message, NewObjectInTeam, NewObjectInProject, ObjectActivity, Promotion, PullRequestStatus, ReportStatus, Run, Schedule, Security, Streak, SystemAlert, Transfer, UserInvite). These reflected the old Vrooli web app's product surfaces. The initiative has decided on event-glob subscriptions on vrooli-events (e.g., 'agent-manager.run.*'), which is open-ended. Need to settle how 'category' survives, because rate limits and unsubscribe scopes in both the legacy code and the existing Go scenario reference category as a first-class dimension.

options.label: Drop the closed enum entirely. 'Category' becomes a free-form string tag the publisher includes in the event payload (e.g., 'transactional', 'marketing', 'security'). Rate limits and unsubscribe scopes operate on these tags but accept any string
options.rationale: Maximally portable; new scenarios can mint new tags without coordinating with notification-hub; matches the open-ended event-glob model

options.label: Preserve a small canonical set (e.g., 'transactional', 'marketing', 'security', 'product', 'system') as a recommended-but-not-enforced taxonomy, with publishers free to add their own
options.rationale: Gives users a meaningful default unsubscribe-by-category UX without forcing every publisher to invent its own taxonomy

options.label: Keep category as a closed enum but make it scenario-extensible via configuration (each profile declares its own category list)
options.rationale: Strict typing within a profile, but cross-tenant analytics get harder; adds config surface

items.context: Legacy notify.ts had three modes (default/force_push/prefer_websocket) that suppressed push when the user was actively connected via WebSocket — saving push budget and avoiding double-notification. The greenfield has no WebSocket assumption (it is a portable microservice subscribing to vrooli-events). Need to decide whether/how this 'don't push to actively-present users' policy survives.

options.label: Drop server-side presence tracking. Make this a per-subscription preference: each subscription declares 'always push', 'in-app only', or 'push if no in-app feed activity in last N seconds'. Hub honors it without tracking presence itself
options.rationale: Keeps the hub stateless w.r.t. presence; pushes the policy to the subscription-config layer where users already manage preferences

options.label: Track lightweight presence inside the hub via the in-app feed connection (SSE/poll heartbeat). Suppress push automatically when last-heartbeat < threshold
options.rationale: Smarter default — feels right out of the box without per-subscription config — but adds presence-tracking surface and a new failure mode

options.label: Drop the concept entirely. Always send to all configured channels; if the user wants in-app-only, they unsubscribe push for that category
options.rationale: Simplest possible model; loses some UX polish but eliminates a whole sub-system

items.context: Legacy notify.ts had a sophisticated <Label|Type:ID> deferred-resolution system: variable values containing placeholders triggered batch DB fetches in the user's preferred language at delivery time. This was great for stale-safe i18n but required direct DB access from the notification worker plus a model registry. The greenfield is portable and event-driven; the publisher (e.g., agent-manager) holds the source-of-truth strings. Need to decide how variables resolve.

options.label: Caller-supplied resolved strings only. The notification-hub treats template variables as opaque pre-localized strings. Publishers must call i18n.resolve() before publishing. Greenfield templates use simple {{var}} substitution (matches existing Go scenario at processor.go:455-463)
options.rationale: Portable, simple, no cross-service coupling; matches the event-driven boundary; aligns with the existing Go scenario's renderTemplate

options.label: Caller-supplied strings + an optional resolver-callback registration: profiles can register an HTTP resolver endpoint that the hub calls at delivery time for placeholders matching a registered prefix
options.rationale: Preserves the deferred-resolution superpower for tenants that want it, without coupling the hub to any specific data source

options.label: Per-channel content blocks instead of variable substitution: templates carry rendered HTML/text/push-payload per channel, no substitution at all in the hub; publishers do all rendering
options.rationale: Maximally minimal hub responsibility; pushes complexity to publishers but is the cleanest separation

items.text: Catalog of legacy NotificationCategory enum (notify.ts:117-135): AccountCreditsOrApi, Award, IssueStatus, Message, NewObjectInTeam, NewObjectInProject, ObjectActivity, Promotion, PullRequestStatus, ReportStatus, Run, Schedule, Security, Streak, SystemAlert, Transfer, UserInvite. Each had a corresponding pushFoo() helper (31 helpers total at notify.ts:740-1280) wired to specific i18next translation keys. These represent the actual product event surfaces of the old web app — useful as a reference list of 'what kinds of notifications a real product sends', but a closed enum does not fit the open event-glob subscription model the initiative has chosen.

Push device schema is Web Push spec (RFC 8030 + VAPID). Legacy push_device fields: endpoint (string), p256dh (string), auth (string), expires (datetime). These port verbatim to SQLite. APNs (device_token + bundle_id + env) and FCM (registration_token) variants fit the same device table with a 'kind' discriminator. Recommend a unified devices table: (id, profile_id, contact_id, kind, endpoint_or_token, keys_jsonb, expires, last_verified_at, last_used_at, status).

Legacy daily-limit pattern (notify.ts:333-389) uses redisClient.incr('notification:{userId}:{category}') with 24h expire and a deliberate fail-silent fallback (when Redis is unavailable, suppress the notification rather than risk spam). For the SQLite-only greenfield: a counters table keyed by (profile_id, contact_id, category_or_channel, period_bucket) with periodic GC achieves the same semantics. Cost-based limits (in the spec but missing from legacy) need an additional 'cost' column accumulated on each successful send.

Lifecycle state divergence: existing Go scenario uses pending/processing/delivered/failed (4 states; processor.go:158, 482-512). The research spec calls for pending/queued/sending/sent/delivered/failed (6 states). Legacy TS had no explicit state enum — it relied on BullMQ queue state plus DB record presence. The 6-state model separates 'in our queue' (queued) from 'handed to provider' (sending) from 'provider ack' (sent) from 'recipient confirmed' (delivered), which is significantly more useful for observability and partial-failure analytics. Recommend adopting the 6-state model in the domain doc.

Routing primitives in legacy NotifyResult (notify.ts:541-720) — toUser, toUsers, toTeam, toOwner, toSubscribers, toChatParticipants, toAll — are Vrooli-domain-specific (Team, Owner, ChatParticipant are old Vrooli web concepts). In the event-driven greenfield, recipient resolution happens via subscriptions on event glob patterns; the hub does not need these primitives. The 'fan-out to a group' concern belongs to the publisher (or to vrooli-events itself, e.g., as an event metadata audience hint). Recommend dropping all of these from the hub's API surface and documenting this as an explicit non-goal.

Existing scenarios/notification-hub/ Go API already implements a usable subset of the domain: Profile (with bcrypt API key), Contact (with timezone, locale, channels, preferences), Template (channels[], category, subject, content, status), Notification (with channels_requested[]/channels_attempted[], priority, scheduled_at, status), NotificationRequest. PRD lists DND/quiet hours, frequency limits, full unsubscribe management as P0-not-implemented. The greenfield rewrite is justified by architectural changes (drop n8n/Postgres/Redis, adopt SQLite/ntfy/vrooli-events, define proto contract), not by a fundamental redesign of these domain primitives — they should largely carry forward with the adjustments noted in decisions D2-D4.
